newsitem.title: USA: Capsized chemical barge righted on Mississippi.
newsitem.headline: Capsized chemical barge righted on Mississippi.

text.p: A sky-blue chemical fog that intermittently plagued local residents near the Mississippi River for 11 days appeared to dissipate Friday after a capsized barge was righted, authorities said.

Coast Guard spokesman Chris Haley told Reuters the barge was righted without incident by two cranes brought downriver from Vicksburg, Miss. "There has been vapor in the area around the barge but it hasn't spread to land," he said.
The barge, containing a volatile mix of benzene and gasoline, overturned March 17 after a tugboat with 25 barges in tow hit a bridge while trying to negotiate a sharp curve in the river.

The fast river current, swollen to its fourth-highest level this century with flood waters from the Ohio Valley, was blamed in part for the incident and several other maritime accidents that have snarled marine traffic from Baton Rouge to the mouth of the river below New Orleans for almost two weeks, Coast Guard officials said.

In West Baton Rouge Parish, where 65 people had been evacuated since the barge overturned, a deputy sheriff told Reuters late Friday, "It's finally over, thank God! That sucker is right-side up and moving downriver, and our folks are going back home."

As authorities struggled for more than a week to unload the hazardous cargo safely, the fog, containing some benzene and hydrocarbon vapors, intermittently rolled across the Southern University campus and residential neighborhoods in the northern part of the city and communities on the west bank of the river.
The campus was evacuated twice and other residents were ordered to stay inside with windows and doors closed.
More than 386 people were treated at local hospitals for nausea, headaches, respiratory problems and eye, nose and throat irritation, hospital officials said.

State authorities were forced to close highways and bridges whenever the blue clouds appeared, and twice evacuated state office buildings downtown. Thousands of students got an extra day or two of Easter holidays after city officials closed 37 schools they feared might be affected by the vapors.

Ten lawsuits already have been filed in connection with the incident and the barge owners have petitioned in federal court to have their damages limited to the value of the barge and cargo, a provision written into law more than a century ago to protect the nation's fledgling maritime industry.

Corps of Engineers spokesman Rob Brown told Reuters the Mississippi River crested at Baton Rouge Thursday night slightly below the expected level. "So far, all the levees have held, and we think the worst may be over -- for now," he said. "We'll just have to wait and see what happens when we normally get high water in May."
